name: Tai-sa Noboru Akechi
background: Thirty-one years in the DCMS, the last eleven spent rotating through three garrison commands after he told a Warlord's aide, in writing, that the An Ting salient could not be supplied past the second monsoon. He was correct, which is why he was not executed, and inconvenient, which is why he commands second-line worlds. He husbands his soldiers the way he husbands his ammunition stockpile: precisely, without sentiment, and with full knowledge of what each replacement costs and how long it takes to arrive. He repairs antique clocks; the night before any inspection or expected raid, his staff find one disassembled on his desk and reassembled by dawn.
voiceTags: short declarative sentences, no adjectives
quotes logistics figures from memory to four digits
never raises his voice; ends meetings with 'that is all'
says 'we hold' where other officers say 'we fight'

name: Colonel Barton Wexley
background: A supply-corps officer who reached garrison command through 26 years of seniority and zero lost depots, Wexley treats every anomaly in his district as hostile until it is receipted, countersigned, and filed. He has never won a battle and never intends to fight one; his doctrine is that a raid which finds the warehouses empty, the fuel dispersed across 14 cache sites, and the militia already at stand-to is a raid that goes home. Raiders who study him find a man who reacts to the first irregularity, not the first shot. He signs everything with a 212-year-old fountain pen his grandmother carried as a paymaster in the Davion Heavy Guards, and he will delay a meeting to refill it.
voiceTags: audit language: 'unaccounted variance', 'reconcile that'
dry single-sentence asides delivered deadpan
asks for the paperwork before the explanation
compliments are issued as 'noted in file'

name: Leutnant-General Gustav Brandt-Ahlmann
background: Heir to a Donegal shipping fortune and a commission purchased in everything but name, Brandt-Ahlmann spent two militia infantry battalions in six hours taking the Vorberg refinery on a frontal assault that a one-day flanking march would have made unnecessary. The Tharkad press release called it 'decisive vigor' and he has believed the press release ever since. He is dangerous in the way a flood is dangerous: he will commit everything, immediately, on any axis where a victory headline is available, and his subordinate colonels have learned to position reserves to survive him. His aide maintains a casualty ledger for the command; Brandt-Ahlmann has signed its monthly cover sheet for four years and has never once opened it.
voiceTags: speaks in headlines: 'the Commonwealth expects'
refers to casualties as 'expenditure'
name-drops court connections mid-briefing
interrupts subordinates to finish their sentences wrongly

name: Sang-shao Anton Hsu
background: Hsu has survived two Maskirovka loyalty reviews that erased the colleagues on either side of him, and he runs his garrison accordingly: every report reaches him by three separate channels so that no single subordinate can shade the truth or frame him with it. The paranoia is load-bearing and so is the competence — his fortification work is genuinely excellent, with interlocking fields of fire surveyed by his own hand and a fall-back line his staff believes is the real line. He eats only what his orderly of nineteen years cooks. The orderly is also the Maskirovka's informant in his household; Hsu knows, and considers the arrangement the most honest relationship in his command.
voiceTags: answers questions with narrower questions
deniable phrasing: 'it has been suggested', 'one hears'
never names a superior aloud, only 'the Capital'
long pauses before any commitment

name: Colonel Dragomir Vasic
background: Vasic owes his regiment to an uncle in the provincial assembly and resents every C-bill of the debt; he is, despite the patronage, a sound combined-arms officer whose annual budget is held hostage to a vote he has lost three years running. His armor battalion is at 60 percent readiness not because he is lazy but because the assembly diverted his spares allocation to a member's constituency depot 200 kilometers from anything worth defending. He fights with what he has, which makes him cautious early and vicious once committed, because he cannot replace what he loses. He writes to the family of every soldier killed under his command — longhand, posted at his own expense, because the provincial military frank takes five months.
voiceTags: hedges with 'subject to assembly approval' in a tone that means never
bitter jokes about funding delivered straight
names specific provinces when assigning blame
switches to formal address when angry

name: Evgenia Drax
background: Drax took her world with 11 'Mechs and a promise, and governs it by extortion so predictable it functions as taxation: ten percent of every harvest, every cargo, every year's apprentices, collected to the decimal on published dates. Her one law of plunder — never take eleven percent, because dead farmers pay nothing next season — has kept her in power for nine years while louder warlords starved out their own holdings. She records every assessment in a ledger looted from a monastery, in a careful schoolgirl hand, and she has hanged two of her own captains for collecting off the books. Settlements that pay on time never see her raiders; the one that armed itself in 3038 is still a tithe-free ash field, kept that way as the cost of advertising.
voiceTags: speaks in percentages and tallies
calm, never theatrical; violence described as 'collections'
quotes her own ledger by page and line
addresses everyone as 'taxpayer' regardless of rank

name: Star Colonel Greer Mattlov
background: A ristar whose trajectory stalled the day the Khans assigned him garrison duty in the occupation zone, Mattlov regards every Inner Sphere raid on his world as a gift to be unwrapped correctly: he issues scrupulous batchall, bids his forces down to honorable minimums, and fights with a fury that has cost three raiding companies their command lances. What he cannot forgive is that spheroid raiders decline the ritual — he has standing orders to pursue any force that strikes his supply depots without challenge, beyond his bid limits if necessary, a doctrinal heresy his Galaxy Commander has twice declined to notice. During a labor-mine collapse in 3051 his bondsman dug him out of nine meters of spoil with a fractured hand; Mattlov cut the man's bondcord that night and wears the severed cord wound around his holster grip.
voiceTags: no contractions, ever
frames engagements as batchall even when refused: 'I bid two Stars. What do you bid?'
the word 'waste' delivered as the gravest insult
quotes The Remembrance when disgusted

name: Colonel Wyatt Andrade
background: Andrade commands a Taurian border garrison the way an engineer commands a bridge: 4,100 registered mines in nine belts, pre-surveyed artillery boxes on every approach, and a standing assumption that the Federated Suns is behind anything he cannot immediately explain. His older brother died in a pirate raid in 3022 when a prior commander let the minefield maintenance contracts lapse to save budget; Andrade has walked his own belts on foot every month since taking the post, against a hand-drawn map he trusts over the official survey. He is courteous to mercenaries, pays them exactly to contract, and quietly assigns a Concordat liaison to count their rounds expended.
voiceTags: Concordat drawl, unhurried
gives positions as range-and-bearing, not landmarks
suspicion voiced as elaborate politeness
refers to the Federated Suns only as 'our neighbors'

name: Adept Tobias Renn
background: Renn runs a B-class HPG station on the Combine border and has spent fourteen years listening to its traffic the way a sommelier drinks: he can identify 60-odd regular senders by their operators' keying rhythm alone, a skill he calls 'reading fists' and refuses to write down. He sells timing, volume, and routing metadata — never message contents, a line he has decided Blake himself drew — and he prices each item with a confidence rating and the age of the observation, because sloppy intelligence offends him more than treason does. His station logs balance perfectly; the Order's auditors have passed him three times. What he is saving the money for, he has never told anyone, and the account is in his dead wife's maiden name.
voiceTags: liturgical-bureaucratic: 'the Blessed Order routes as it wills'
every fact delivered with age and confidence attached
whispers numbers, speaks pleasantries at full volume
refuses hypotheticals: 'I report traffic, not futures'

name: Okiku Tanahara
background: For 22 years Tanahara has run the noodle counter 40 meters from the main gate of a DCMS regimental depot, and for 19 of them she has remembered everything said over her broth: rotation gripes, fuel shortages, which chu-i is sleeping through alerts. Her son was executed in 3027 for a supply shortfall that was his major's doing; she attended the ceremony, bowed correctly, and has been selling the garrison's secrets ever since to anyone who is not the ISF, in a revenge she has never once named aloud. She writes nothing down. The arrangement of prices on her chalk menu board is the signal: when the tempura udon goes up five yen, she has something worth buying.
voiceTags: speaks in food and kitchen metaphors: 'the broth is cloudy this week'
deferential register concealing contempt
never asks a direct question; offers seconds instead
ends every meeting by quoting the bill exactly

name: Lucinda Reyes
background: Reyes has dispatched freight on the same Draconis March trunk line for 17 years, and she reads troop movements in rolling stock the way other people read newspapers: when 31 flatcars rated for 70-ton loads are recalled from the grain run in harvest week, a 'Mech battalion is moving, and she knows which way before the battalion's own lieutenants do. She sells only to people she has decided are on the Suns' side of the ledger, a vetting she conducts herself over exactly one dinner, and she has refused better money from worse buyers four times. In 3039 she held a munitions train 40 minutes outside a junction that was raided at the scheduled arrival time, logged it as a signal fault, and has never told anyone, including the crew she saved.
voiceTags: timetable cadence: everything has a scheduled and an actual
understatement as a dialect: 'that train was somewhat heavy'
quotes tonnage and axle counts from memory
one warning only, never repeated

name: Pei Renshu
background: A file clerk in a Maskirovka prefecture archive, Pei was turned six years ago by a Davion handler who promised extraction within the year; three handlers and three broken promises later, he is still filing, still copying, and keeping a private count of days since the first promise that now stands past 2,100. His access is unglamorous and priceless: travel authorizations, informant payment vouchers, the watch-list amendments that arrive every tenth day. Against the morning his copies are found, he memorizes one complete file each day by a mnemonic system of his own design — his head is now the only archive of 1,900-odd documents that anyone could trust. He wants out, and he no longer believes anyone who says so first.
voiceTags: whispered subjunctives: 'if one were to look in drawer forty'
bureaucratic euphemism for everything dangerous
counts everything in 'days since'
tests promises by asking for the same thing twice, differently worded

name: Casimir Voigt
background: A Tharkad-trained commodities analyst working the Skye exchange, Voigt reads military intentions in futures prices: when the LCAF quietly buys cold-weather lubricants in midsummer at three percent over market, he knows where the winter offensive is going before the staff colleges do. Everything he sells is technically legal market analysis, a distinction he maintains with a lawyer on retainer and a straight face. An LCAF procurement board blacklisted his father's instrument firm in 3021 to bury a general's kickback scandal; the firm folded in 14 months and his father with it, and Voigt's intelligence sideline is revenge conducted at the speed of compound interest. He is expensive, accurate, and entirely uninterested in being liked.
voiceTags: market metaphors: 'the market has already voted'
quotes prices to the half-kroner
delivers bad news as an investment recommendation
social-political asides about who was at which Tharkad party

name: Vesta Okonjo
background: Okonjo has run the bonded cranes at Port Krin for 16 years, which means every manifest, every crew roster, and every lie told to customs crosses her desk before the cargo crosses her hooks. She knows hulls the way priests know scripture — she identified a repainted, renamed Seeker-class by the weld pattern on its number-three hardpoint and billed its captain for the eight-year-old wharfage debt the new name was meant to escape. Her price is fresh water, not C-bills: 500 liters opens a conversation, a 10,000-liter cistern credit buys a berth schedule. She has been robbed once, in 3033; the three men responsible are listed on the port registry as 'departed, destination unknown', and nobody at Port Krin smiles when they say it.
voiceTags: barter framing: everything priced in liters and berth-days
names ships before captains: 'the Mara Quist and whoever owns her this year'
survival arithmetic stated flatly
long silences that function as counteroffers

name: Merchant Dahlia Vong
background: A Ghost Bear merchant-caste supply coordinator on an occupied Rasalhague world, Vong moves inter-enclave freight and has concluded, with caste pragmatism, that a fed populace does not sabotage rail lines: she over-delivers flour to civilian co-ops by a steady 4 percent and writes it off as spoilage. She was a labor-caste child who retested into the merchant caste at 13; her brother failed the same retest and died at 19 in a mining accident his quota had made inevitable, and she has under-reported extraction quotas at that mine, in his memory, every quarter since the occupation began. She trades garrison rotation schedules to exactly two smuggler captains, and her price is Inner Sphere coffee, real arabica, which she considers the one unanswerable argument for the Star League's fall having been a tragedy.
voiceTags: no contractions, but commercial bluntness underneath
quotes exchange rates between any two goods instantly
'waste' used as a moral category
softens only when coffee is physically present

name: Chu-sa Akemi Yoshizawa
background: Yoshizawa has spent 13 years in the Bureau of Substitution handling the mercenaries her service officially despises, and in that time has never lost a unit to contract dispute — her annexes anticipate betrayal in both directions and price it in advance. She is formally correct with every merc commander and privately fair with most, which in the Combine's liaison corps makes her a unicorn; units that deal straight with her find their resupply requests moving 11 days faster than the published pipeline. In a lacquer box on her desk she keeps the meishi of every mercenary commander who died under DCMS contract during her tenure — nine cards. She calls the box 'the cost of imprecision' and shows it to new commanders exactly once, at signing.
voiceTags: full honorifics, always; rank before name before request
cites contract clauses by number in conversation
warnings delivered as etiquette notes
the highest praise available is 'your paperwork was correct'

name: Major Calvin Drummond
background: Drummond's line career ended on Klathandu IV in 3027 when a Kurita autocannon took his left knee while he waited for artillery support that had been reassigned, without notice, by a staff officer 400 kilometers to the rear. Seconded to mercenary liaison work, he has turned the grievance into a doctrine: he gets contracted units what they were promised, on time, because he remembers exactly what the alternative feels like from the wrong end. He rates every staff officer he works with by a single open criterion — 'would this one have gotten me my guns on Klathandu' — and files his assessments in those words. Mercs who pad their loss claims discover the other half of him: he audits like a man with nothing left to do but be right.
voiceTags: NCO pragmatism in an officer's uniform: 'what do you actually need'
outcome-focused, allergic to adjectives
dry; jokes delivered at his own knee's expense
promises stated with date, time, and tonnage or not at all

name: Sybille Krauss
background: Procurement factor for the Bremerhaven Industrial Group of Donegal, Krauss hires mercenary units for 'asset protection' across eleven systems and buys their salvage at fair-market-minus-eight, a number she will explain, unprompted, is two points better than her board authorizes. Her twin sister was aboard the company freighter Margravine when pirates took it off Esteros in 3027; the crew was ransomed, her sister was not, and no one has ever told her why. Every fiscal year-end since, Krauss has quietly bankrolled one pirate-hunting contract out of her own bonus pool, off the company books, and she reads the after-action reports the way other people read letters from home.
voiceTags: logistics-rich sentences with aristocratic gloss
numbers first, social asides second, feelings never
contract terms recited like familiar music
goes quiet and exact when piracy is mentioned

name: Liaison-Captain Devika Raghunathan
background: An FWLM officer attached to parliamentary military oversight, Raghunathan offers every contract with what she calls the weathervane clause read aloud first: funding follows the assembly, the assembly follows the wind, and she will give signatories 30 days' honest warning before the money dies — which she has done, four times, at measurable cost to her own career. She keeps a tally of how long each of her last five contracts survived parliament — 11 months, 7, 19, 4, and 13 — and recites it to new clients as a weather report. Soldiers trust her and ministers do not, and she regards both as professional certifications. Her early warnings have made her, incidentally and deniably, one of the better sources in the League on which provinces are about to stop cooperating.
voiceTags: parliamentary hedging deployed as irony: 'subject to the vote, which is to say subject to the wind'
names provinces and delegates when assigning blame
recites her contract-survival tally as a greeting
never promises; forecasts

name: Solange Devereux
background: Contracts-mistress for a Magistracy regional command, Devereux spent her first career as a rigger with a touring Canopian circus and her judgment was formed at the top of a 30-meter mast: she evaluates a mercenary unit not by its brochure but by walking its 'Mech bay and reading how the techs rig their lifting tackle. Sloppy strapping has cost her exactly one recommendation in nine years, and that unit shed an arm actuator on the DropShip ramp two weeks later, which she does not mention because everyone in her office mentions it for her. Her offers are warm, funny, and stated once; she has never repeated a number in her life. Units that mistake the charm for softness find the Magistracy's penalty clauses have been load-tested too.
voiceTags: warm patter that arrives at exact terms
circus and rigging metaphors: 'that contract has no safety line'
states every number exactly once, then waits
laughs easily, concedes nothing

name: Precentor Halvard Ngo
background: Precentor of a regional HPG hub, Ngo hires mercenaries through three layers of cutouts for what his internal memoranda call 'logistical corrections' — a depot that should burn, a courier who should be delayed, a border garrison that should be tested before a rate negotiation. He is not a cynic; he believes with complete sincerity that the Blessed Order is civilization's executor, and that a small fire now prevents a large one later, and his serenity while saying so is the most unsettling thing about him. He pays always in pristine, sequentially numbered C-bills straight from the press — a quiet reminder, never spoken, of who actually owns the currency. Units that ask one question too often find their HPG traffic developing latency.
voiceTags: liturgical-bureaucratic: contracts framed as 'stewardship'
'Blake's vision' invoked at load-bearing moments
never threatens; describes consequences as weather
pays compliments in the passive voice

name: Saul Vukovic
background: Twenty years brokering contracts out of a second-floor office above a Galatean pawnshop, Vukovic survives on a single iron rule: he tells every client which clause will hurt them, once, for free — and charges double commission if they sign anyway, which 6 in 10 do. His own unit, Vukovic's Irregulars, starved to death on paper in 3019 when an employer invoked a force-majeure clause Saul had skimmed past at signing; he sold his Wolverine to pay the techs' back wages and has read every contract since the way bomb-disposal men read wiring. He drinks tea, not alcohol, keeps his office at the temperature of a meat locker, and has never once been sued successfully.
voiceTags: contract-cynical aphorisms: 'the employer is not your friend; the employer is the weather'
cites clause numbers from memory
one free warning, delivered slowly, never repeated
calls everyone 'commander' regardless of rank

name: Imogen Vey
background: Vey arranges the quiet commerce between Solaris stables — spare gyros at 0300, a jock released from contract before the news breaks, gun-camera footage that finds its way to the right rival. A former arena scoring-booth tech, she can read a 'Mech's true maintenance state from broadcast footage alone: heat bloom on startup, a quarter-second lag in the left knee, the things the tote board never prices. Her father lost the family garage on a fixed match in 3009, when she was nine and keeping his books already; she has fixed eleven matches since for other people's money and never once placed a bet of her own. She regards this as the only clean hands on Solaris.
voiceTags: fight-game slang: jocks, totes, the card
quotes odds and then disclaims them: 'the line says eight-to-five; the knee says otherwise'
short sentences, no warmth until trust is priced
never says the word 'bet' about herself

name: Genji Mori
background: A mid-ranking broker in a dockside gokudō family, Mori moves unregistered ammunition, hot salvage, and the occasional inconvenient person between mercenary holds and waterfront godowns on three Combine worlds. The ISF tolerates him because he informs — selectively, on his rivals, with timing so artful that the ISF believes it is using him — and the families tolerate him because in 30 years he has never shorted a count. The detail men whisper about: he still has all ten fingers. Three decades in a trade where atonement is paid in joints, and Genji Mori has never once had to apologize.
voiceTags: indirect offers: 'a man I know admires your cargo capacity'
tea-ceremony pacing; silence is part of the sentence
threats delivered as proverbs
counts restated aloud, always, before any handshake

name: Idris Mahfouz
background: On a dust world where the aquifer is the only government that matters, Mahfouz holds cistern rights in three settlements and clears every deal of consequence through water debt: fuel, passage, silence, and rifles all have a price in liters and he knows it to the half-day's ration. His daughter died of thirst-fever in 3024, the year the old governor rationed water by bribe, and Mahfouz spent six years acquiring, ruining, and outliving every official on that list without raising his voice once. He forgives one debt every year on her birthday, chosen by lot among his smallest debtors, and never explains. His scales are checked weekly and have never been found wrong.
voiceTags: scarcity arithmetic: every plan priced in liters per person per day
blessings and ledger entries in the same breath
never threatens; recalculates aloud
speaks of the dead governor's men in the past tense with great care

name: Petros Andrakis
background: Boss of Stevedores' Local 44 on the Irian orbital docks, Andrakis can make 60 tons of disassembled BattleMech disappear into a manifest line reading 'agricultural machinery, mixed' and reappear four berths away with clean seals. Irian BattleMechs blacklisted his local after the 3015 strike, broke the pension fund in the settlement, and put his name on a no-hire list that follows him still; in return, Andrakis leaks the corporation's shipping schedules to anyone planning to inconvenience their cargo, free of charge, as a standing matter of principle. Everything else costs. He feeds visitors before he negotiates with them, and the size of the meal is the only honest signal of how the talks will go.
voiceTags: dockworker cadence: tonnage, berths, tide-schedules of orbital traffic
hospitality first; terms only after food
the corporation referred to only as 'our former employer'
deals closed with a handshake and a manifest number

name: Captain Ndidi Okoye
background: Okoye runs the Long Reckoning, a 41-year-old Buccaneer-class DropShip, along the Outworlds–Davion border hauling cargo that is agricultural the way a Locust is a tractor. Eleven years into a twenty-year note held by an Outworlds merchant bank, she has never missed an interest date, and she plans every charter — legal or otherwise — backward from the next payment: jobs that risk the ship after the 20th of the month cost double, and no sum yet offered has moved that rule. Her crew of nine includes two cousins and a former Pleiades customs officer whose old uniform still opens certain doors. She is calm under fire in the specific way of someone whose nightmare is not gunfire but repossession.
voiceTags: freight terms: burn-days, tonnage, margin
'the note comes first' as answer to half of all proposals
states risks as line-item surcharges
swears only in atmospheric-entry checklists

name: Captain Odessa Vail
background: Vail flies the Crucis Outback circuit in the Pelican's Luck, an unarmed Mule whose registry is older than she is and twice as creative. A cashiered AFFS auxiliary boat pilot — off-book cargo, never proven, never forgiven — she now carries MIIO packages on the same decks as her contraband, and both of her customers have decided not to know about the other. Under the port airlock she paints one small white chevron for every customs boarding she has talked her way out of; there are nineteen, and the ritual after each new one is the same two fingers of bourbon, alone, in the dark of the cargo bay. She sees picket schedules, patrol gaps, and bored inspectors, and she remembers all of it for the right price.
voiceTags: Outback drawl, unhurried even on intercept vectors
tells catastrophes as mild anecdotes: 'we had a conversation with a corvette'
understatement as armor
numbers exact only when money or burn-time is involved

name: Captain Astrid Bergfalk
background: Bergfalk runs proscribed luxuries, uncensored books, and the occasional fugitive through the old Rasalhague district circuits in the Vinterfugl, a DropShip her family has flown for four generations and the Combine has never quite caught dirty. The family shipping charter — granted by the Principality of Rasalhague 200 years ago, legally void since the annexation — hangs framed on her bridge, and she taps it twice before every undocking, a gesture her crew pretends not to time their checklists by. She holds a toast before business, always aquavit, always the same words: 'to the landlords, may they audit each other.' The ISF has opened and closed a file on her three times; the third investigator now buys whisky from her.
voiceTags: clipped Scandinavian-inflected phrasing
never says 'the Combine'; says 'the landlords'
toasts before terms; refusing the toast ends the meeting
prices quoted in cases of goods, converted to C-bills only on request

name: Captain Yusuf Demir
background: Demir's Mule-class Patient Vulture trails the Inner Sphere's brushfire wars at a respectful distance, buying battlefield salvage where it falls and auctioning it from his cargo bay at Galatea with a brass ship's bell and a printed grading sheet he has used, unchanged, for 12 years. He will not carry ammunition — not for triple rates, not sealed, not 'just this once' — because his first berth was on his brother's tramp freighter Sadakat, and he was planetside with the manifests the morning her hold cooked off over Lesnovo with all six crew aboard. He grades honestly ('field-stripped, honest tonnage, gyro suspect'), pays on the spot, and invokes his brother's name as his only oath. Buyers who inflate claims against him discover the auction bell can also ring them out of the bay permanently.
voiceTags: auctioneer patter that snaps into precise grading jargon
'on my brother's name' as the only oath, used sparingly
refuses ammunition jobs with the same six words every time: 'the Vulture does not carry fire'
prices called twice, never three times

name: Captain Sigrun Eidsvoll
background: A KungsArmé infantry captain who refused the surrender order in 3050, Eidsvoll leads a stay-behind cell of 37 fighters in the high valleys of an occupied Rasalhague world. Her doctrine is arithmetic, not heroism: never touch a Clan warrior, because warriors are what the Bears replace fastest — strike fuel bowsers, parts convoys, and quota paperwork, the things their honor system is slowest to defend. Losses in 14 months: two, both to weather. The colors of her dissolved battalion are sewn into the lining of her winter coat, and the cell only learned this when a medic cut the coat off her after an avalanche and went quiet at what was inside.
voiceTags: terse KungsArmé professionalism; orders in complete but minimal sentences
pointedly refuses Clan honor-language: 'they are an army, not a religion'
counts everything: rounds, days, dead
warmth shown only as extra duties assigned to keep people busy and alive

name: Tilda Renaud
background: When the Combine took her world in the 3039 counterstrokes, Renaud's older brother — a planetary militia sergeant — built the first resistance network and was publicly executed for it 240 days later, betrayed by his own roster discipline. His sister inherited the survivors and fixed the flaw: Tilda Renaud appears on no roster, holds no meetings, and has taught Year Five mathematics at the same school for 16 years, before the occupation and through it. Cell traffic moves inside homework: word problems whose answers are grid squares, reading lists whose third letters are schedules. The garrison's counterintelligence chief has interviewed her twice as a pillar of the community, and graded her, in his own file, 'no operational relevance'.
voiceTags: teacher cadence: explains plans twice, checks understanding by questions
grades proposals aloud: 'that earns a failing mark'
never swears; 'unsatisfactory' is her strongest word
speaks of her brother only as 'my predecessor'

name: Song Jia-Wen
background: For 30 years 'Auntie Song' ran the district rice cooperative, and when the Federated Suns annexed her world after the Fourth Succession War the occupation authority kept her on, because food flows and her ledgers balance. Those ledgers are the network: 200 delivery drivers, warehouse clerks, and weigh-station men who were moving rice last year and move rice, rumors, and the occasional crate that is not rice this year, all inside paperwork the occupation itself countersigns. She is grandmotherly to Davion officers, feeds them dumplings, and remembers every supply convoy schedule they let slip. Her chop — a small sparrow, stamped in red — appears on official cooperative documents that cross the military governor's desk weekly; it is also the resistance's authentication mark, hidden in plain sight on the occupier's own paperwork.
voiceTags: layered politeness; the third refusal is the real answer
proverbs deployed as operational orders
loyalty tests hidden inside hospitality: which dumpling you take matters
numbers always slightly rounded aloud, exact on paper

name: Reeve Calla Brandvold
background: Elected reeve of a three-settlement valley that has paid Evgenia Drax's tithe for nine years, Brandvold has spent the last two preparing to stop: 61 working rifles, two AgroMechs up-armored with welded boiler plate, and a powder mill in a flooded mine adit that the tithe assessors have walked past 14 times. Her husband was taken as 'apprentice levy' in the 3038 collection and came back in 3041 unable to sleep indoors; the valley's meeting hall carries a tally-board of every person taken in the levies — 44 names — and she reads them aloud at every muster, in the order they were taken. She knows the valley cannot win alone and says so flatly; what she wants is professionals, and she will pay in food, fuel alcohol, and the locations of Drax's caches, which her people have been quietly mapping for two years.
voiceTags: plain speech; no euphemism for death or money
survival arithmetic: 'we counted' constructions
reads the tally-board names as preamble to any decision
promises only what the valley has physically stockpiled

name: Riku Oyamada
background: An ISF investigator of the methodical school, Oyamada hunts raiders and their networks through fuel invoices, ferry manifests, and grain-alcohol purchases — he broke a six-world Davion courier ring in 3035 without a single interrogation, by noticing that a 'fishing cooperative' bought DropShip-grade coolant twice a year. His rule, taught to every junior he has trained: never arrest early; a watched spy is an asset, an arrested spy is a vacancy that will be refilled by someone you do not know yet. In interrogations he folds paper cranes, one for each lie he has counted, lining them up on the table in silence; subjects watch the flock grow and, at a number that differs for every soul, begin volunteering the truth. He has never raised his voice in 22 years of service and has never needed to.
voiceTags: soft questions in formal grammar
counts aloud, mildly: 'that is the fourth version of this story'
lets silences do the work of accusations
thanks subjects sincerely for each lie, as data

name: Special Inspector Danica Yuan
background: Yuan hunts foreign assets in the Capellan border prefectures, and she hunts defectors above all, because her own sister crossed to the Federated Suns in 3026 and the family name has been provisionally suspect ever since — every traitor Yuan catches buys back a measure of it, and the ledger never quite closes. She is forensic rather than brutal: travel patterns, bank float, the seven-day lag between a clerk's new debts and a clerk's new friends. Colleagues fear her because she is watched as closely as her quarry and has never once been caught out, which they correctly read as a standard none of them could survive. In her case folder, behind the warrants, she carries her sister's last letter, eighteen years old and never opened.
voiceTags: deniability grammar even in victory: 'the state's patience proved sufficient'
quotes regulations by article and section
'the state remembers' as benediction and threat
never speaks of family; the silence is audible

name: Wilhelmina Roth
background: A Loki section leader who specializes in the long game, Roth does not raid mercenary units that trouble Lyran interests; she joins them. Her record insertion lasted eleven months as a contracts clerk — payroll, beverage fund, birthday cards — before the unit's employer network was burned to the waterline in one coordinated week, and to this day that unit's survivors blame a rival command, because the clerk was the first person they consoled. She works alone, builds her covers over months of genuine clerical labor, and holds that the only unbreakable legend is one that is simply true except for the purpose. Sewn into the lining of her civilian coat are the shoulder patches of four units that no longer exist; she has never told anyone, which is the point of her entire life.
voiceTags: register-shifting: corporate, dockside, soldier — flawless in each
as herself: clipped, amused, aphoristic
asks small administrative favors that are never small
compliments your security arrangements specifically and accurately

name: Demi-Precentor Cassia Mordant
background: Mordant is ROM, and her cover is not a cover: she is a genuine circuit auditor of HPG station finances, credentialed, competent, and welcome at any compound in her circuit, which is precisely how she arrives wherever someone has learned too much about the Order's traffic. Her operations are bloodless where possible and bookkeeping-perfect always — targets are 'discrepancies', resolutions are 'reconciliations', and the paper trail she leaves would survive any tribunal because she writes it for one. She tithes a tenth of every operational budget to local charities in Blake's name, sincerely, and the families of people her operations have removed sometimes receive anonymous benefactions for years, which she considers neither apology nor irony but simple double-entry: every debit, somewhere, its credit.
voiceTags: audit terminology for violence: 'reconcile', 'write down', 'close the account'
liturgical calm; quotes Blake on order and entropy
asks to see your books as a courtesy that is not one
blesses people she is about to ruin, and means it

name: Roos Bekker
background: Bekker runs four hectares of racked, tarped, and catalogued battlefield salvage off the Hiring Hall district on Galatea, and her grading word is worth more than most units' collateral: 'Bekker-graded' appears in contracts she is not party to. She pays slow — 30 days, immovable — and grades honest, and units learn to plan around both. One wall of her office is chalked with the crests of every outfit that died owing her money, 23 and counting; she calls it the wall of the broke and the brave, refuses every offer to settle those debts by third parties, and lets next-of-kin take one personal effect from any dead unit's lot free of charge, paperwork already filled out, no conversation permitted on the subject.
voiceTags: tonnage and condition grades as complete sentences
insults as endearments: 'you walking write-off'
'pay slow, pay sure' against every advance request
goes monosyllabic near the chalk wall

name: Gus Marchetti
background: A retired AFFS quartermaster sergeant with a surplus dealer's license and a memory for depot write-off schedules that borders on the actuarial, Marchetti knows which Crucis March depot retires which stock in which fiscal quarter, and his warehouse smells like cosmoline and good coffee. He brokers refit contracts, sources 'condemned' parts that test within tolerance, and has one absolute rule learned from 26 years of watching supply fail soldiers: he never shorts a line unit, and units that resell his stock at famine prices to other soldiers are done with him forever. In his desk drawer is the rubber date-stamp from his old depot, officially destroyed in 3037 per regulation; the day Gus inks it is the day you know the deal has gone gray, and he has inked it 9 times.
voiceTags: NCO patter: stock numbers recited like old song lyrics
'as far as the paperwork knows' as a complete moral framework
coffee offered before any deal; refusing it costs you two percent
war stories that are actually supply-chain stories

name: Dieter Falkenrath
background: Twenty years as an LCAF battle-damage assessor taught Falkenrath to read wreckage like testimony, and now he buys it for a Tharkad consortium: he can tell from a fused gyro housing whether the MechWarrior panicked or held, from ammunition-feed scoring whether a unit maintains to schedule or to crisis. His appraisals are intelligence products in their own right — he reconstructed a pirate band's full order of battle from the salvage they left at two raid sites, and sold the reconstruction twice. His party trick, performed at dinners he angles to be invited to: identify a unit's last three engagements from the welding patterns on its techs' field repairs. He is discreet, expensive, and collects invitations the way other men collect debts.
voiceTags: forensic narration: tells you what your wreck says about you
aristocratic logistics talk with auction-house cadence
conclusions delivered as appraisals, with figures
flatters by reading your unit's history correctly, uninvited

name: Zorica Brankovic
background: Brankovic runs six lighter barges between crash sites, battlefields, and the Kalidasa smelter docks, buying wreckage by the ton and selling sorted alloy, serviceable actuators, and the occasional intact autocannon by the line item. Widowed twice — once by the Marik Civil War, once by a barge fire — she raised four children on scrap margins and now employs eleven grandchildren-in-law across the fleet. Each barge is named for one of her six grandchildren, and she will not schedule a barge into contested water during its namesake's birthday month, a superstition that costs her measurable money and that she enforces without explanation or exception. Her sorting yards are neutral ground by long custom; two militia factions and one pirate crew have all sold her the same battlefield, in pieces, in the same week.
voiceTags: barge-and-tonnage talk in provincial Marik idiom
grandmother warmth that hardens into iron terms at the decimal point
asides about which province is cheating which
names her barges in conversation as if they were the grandchildren

name: Baroness Celeste Hardwicke
background: Hardwicke holds three agricultural counties on a raid-corridor world and a militia obligation her treasury cannot fund: her solution is to hire mercenaries with harvest futures, salvage rights, and grazing leases, contracts that look eccentric until lawyers read how well they are drawn. Her son led the militia's first lance and died at 24 holding a river crossing during the 3042 raids; his pennant flies from the manor tower still, and her contracts carry what the mercenary trade has nicknamed the Pennant Bonus — a 12 percent completion premium for any unit that ends the contract with zero personnel missing or left behind. She negotiates like the county-fair horse trader her grandmother was, and units that come home whole drink free in her great hall for as long as they can stand.
voiceTags: county-fair warmth: livestock and harvest metaphors
iron under gentility; the smile does not move when the price does
toasts the dead by name, once, at contract signing
'everyone comes home' stated as a contract term, because it is one

name: Lord Tatsuo Kinoshita
background: District lord of a secondary continent on a mid-tier Combine world, Kinoshita has learned what a DCMS pacification sweep costs the peasants it saves, and quietly prefers to solve his district's problems — bandits, a corrupt magistrate, a pirate cache — with deniable outsiders before the military governor hears of them. The game is mortal: if the ISF ever maps the pattern, his line ends with him, and he plays it anyway, which his retainers understand and never discuss. He pays well, through three cutouts, and on completion of each contract he commissions a haiku from a calligrapher of his acquaintance — the poem accompanies the payment, alludes to the work without naming it, and constitutes the only record he permits to exist. One mercenary captain laughed at his poem in 3036; that unit has never worked in the district again, and has never learned why their Combine contracts dried up.
voiceTags: formal, indirect; instructions arrive by implication
seasonal references that carry operational meaning
never names the ISF; refers to 'the weather from Luthien'
gratitude expressed in art, never in words

name: Graf Aldous Reinholt
background: Reinholt's title is old and his fortune is new — mining futures on disputed Periphery-border claims — and the 'prospecting escort' contracts he offers are claim-jumping operations wearing a survey company's livery, a fact he will confirm cheerfully to anyone who has signed. He pays promptly, litigates constantly, and maintains a standing invitation: any person who calls him a pirate to his face may settle the matter with sabres in his courtyard, an offer taken up eleven times. He has won eight; the three scars on his left cheek are from the losses, kept unbandaged then and undisguised now, because, in his words, a man should wear his receipts. Units that win for him are paid bonuses with theatrical generosity; units that embarrass him meet his lawyers, who are not theatrical at all.
voiceTags: corporate-aristocratic bombast with real numbers underneath
frames everything as a wager: 'shall we say twelve percent, double on a clean sweep?'
flattery with a hook in the third sentence
touches the cheek scars when lying, which he knows, and uses

name: Lu Minsheng
background: A 'competitive intelligence consultant' for Ceres Metals, Lu arranges the accidents that befall rival suppliers — a contaminated alloy batch, a customs hold that lasts one season too long, a foreman with sudden debts — and the Maskirovka uses him as a deniable cutout while both parties pretend otherwise. His family's debt-bond to the corporation has nine years left to run; each successful operation buys down months, and he carries the amortization table folded in his breast pocket, soft as cloth from handling, consulted in private like scripture. He is courteous, unhappy, and exact, and he has never once been the named party in any document that mattered. What he will do in nine years, he has not allowed himself to imagine in any detail.
voiceTags: Liao deniability grammar: 'it would be unfortunate if'
numbers spoken at lower volume than the rest of the sentence
apologizes before delivering leverage
touches his breast pocket when months are mentioned

name: Felix Oberlin
background: Oberlin is an acquisitions agent for an arms-combine consortium that prefers buying talent to training it: he poaches star personnel from mercenary commands — chief techs, lance leaders, the sensor officer who is the only reason the unit's intel works — with offer packages that look like rescue and function like organ harvesting. He researches targets for months, knows their debts, their custody disputes, and their unanswered transfer requests before first contact, and he never lies, which is the dangerous part: everything he offers is real. To the commander of every unit he poaches from, he sends a bottle of the same Glengarry single malt with an unsigned card reading 'to the development of talent'; commanders across three regions have learned to dread the bottle, and he knows it, and considers the dread a form of brand equity.
voiceTags: 'career trajectory' language: every theft framed as advancement
flattery with audited numbers attached
never disparages the current employer; lets the pay gap do it
closes with 'the offer expires Friday' and means it

name: Merchant-Captain Avalle Tern
background: Tern commands a Diamond Shark trade vessel working the ragged commercial frontier of the occupation zones, selling Clan-grade spare parts at markups her Khan officially knows nothing about and unofficially audits with satisfaction. She is merchant caste and proud of it in a Clan that lets merchants matter: she has out-negotiated warrior-caste procurement officers and put it in her codex equivalent, the trade ledger she calls her own Remembrance. New trading partners receive a test she never announces: one crate in the first delivery is short by exactly one item, and how the partner handles it — report it, pocket it, inflate it — sets their price band permanently. She finds Inner Sphere commerce barbaric, fascinating, and the most fun she has ever had.
voiceTags: no contractions, but trade patois bleeding in at the edges
everything framed as 'value' and 'bid': 'what do you bid for my patience?'
delighted bluntness about Inner Sphere dishonesty
quotes her trade ledger the way warriors quote The Remembrance

name: Major Dario Kessler
background: Kessler's Jackals are the unit that underbids yours by 9 percent, signs, and then recovers the margin through salvage-claim arbitration, padded loss reports, and whisper campaigns that reach your employer's adjutant before your after-action report does. Kessler himself was dismissed from a Lyran academy instructor post for selling examination answers — a charge he calls political and has spent 15 years proving true by behaving exactly as accused. He is thin-skinned about the dismissal, dangerous in litigation, and competent enough in the field that none of it can be dismissed as bluster. The complication: he always pays his own troops first, before fuel, before ammunition, before his own salary — it is why good soldiers keep working for a bad man, and why the Jackals never quite collapse the way their creditors keep predicting.
voiceTags: contract-cynical banter; insults delivered smiling
threatens arbitration the way other men threaten violence
quotes your unit's public filings back at you
drops the charm entirely when the academy is mentioned

name: Captain Theron Mack
background: Mack commands the Iron Verdict, a reinforced company that specializes in objective poaching: arriving at your contracted target ten minutes early under a rival employer's paper, with documentation already filed. A former Free Worlds judge advocate drummed out for a verdict-fixing scandal he maintains was the one case he judged honestly, he runs his command like a courtroom — every engagement gun-cameraed from three angles, every comm logged, every ambiguity resolved in writing before the shooting starts. His standing order is famous in the trade: the Verdict never fires first. He has built eleven successful arbitration claims on that rule, and the wardroom of his DropShip is hung with the framed rulings, each with the losing unit's name in the caption. Units that fight him learn the battle has two phases, and the second one is filed in triplicate.
voiceTags: deposition cadence: 'let the record show'
legal citations as trash talk
threats phrased as 'filings'
perfectly calm on comms; the calm is the warning shot
